name: Alpenglow Ridge
description: The last light of the day strikes the peaks first and leaves them last, painting the limestone a deep rose-gold for a few fleeting minutes.
funFact: Alpenglow isn't direct sunlight — it's light scattered back onto the peaks by particles in the air after the sun has already dropped below the horizon.

glossary.meaning: A sedimentary rock made mostly of calcium carbonate, common in mountain ranges like the Dolomites.
A pink or golden glow on mountain peaks caused by sunlight scattering in the atmosphere just before sunrise or after sunset.

name: Understory Light
description: Midday sun breaks through the canopy in shafts, lighting up moss and fern in a temperate rainforest that receives over 150 inches of rain a year.
funFact: This canopy can be so dense that less than 1% of sunlight reaches the forest floor.

glossary.meaning: The uppermost layer of a forest, formed by the spreading branches and leaves of the tallest trees.
A forest type found in cool coastal climates that receives very high annual rainfall, unlike a tropical rainforest.

name: Low Tide Mirror
description: At first light, a receding tide leaves a thin sheet of water on the sand that turns the whole beach into a mirror for the sky.
funFact: This mirror effect only lasts a few minutes each cycle, right as the water film thins to under a millimeter.

glossary.meaning: The regular rise and fall of sea level caused by the gravitational pull of the moon and sun.
When a very thin, still layer of water reflects the sky like glass, briefly turning the beach into a mirror.

name: Cirrus Over the Basin
description: Dry, arid desert air carries almost no moisture to scatter light, so desert sunsets tend to burn a deeper, more saturated orange than anywhere else.
funFact: Clear, dust-free desert air is exactly why desert sunsets often look more saturated than coastal ones.

glossary.meaning: Extremely dry, with little rainfall — the defining trait of a desert climate.
In color, how intense or pure a hue looks, as opposed to washed out or pale.

name: Glacial Blue Hour
description: Once the sun is gone, glacial flour suspended in the lake keeps reflecting the last blue hour light of the sky long after the shore has gone dark.
funFact: The lake's turquoise color comes from finely ground rock particles, called glacial flour, carried down from the glacier above.

glossary.meaning: Finely ground rock dust created by a glacier grinding against bedrock, which gives glacial lakes their turquoise color.
The period of twilight just before sunrise or after sunset when indirect sunlight gives the sky a deep blue tone.

name: First Light on the Firs
description: Fog pools in the low ground overnight, so the first sun of the day only touches the treetops, leaving the trunks still in shadow.
funFact: The Black Forest gets its name from the density of its dark-needled conifers, which can make the canopy look almost black from a distance.

glossary.meaning: Cone-bearing trees, usually evergreen, such as pines, firs, and spruces.
The uppermost layer of a forest, formed by the spreading branches and leaves of the tallest trees.

name: Trailside Clearing
description: An overgrown clearing just off the path, where an old cargo bicycle has been left to rust among the weeds. Someone pauses mid-walk to point out something in the distance.
funFact: Left alone, a metal-frame bicycle like this can take well over a decade to fully rust through in a humid, tropical climate.

glossary.meaning: An open patch of land within a densely vegetated area, often formed where growth has been cut back or trampled down.

name: Ridgeline Blue Hour
description: A silhouette looks out over layered ridgelines toward a coastline in the distance, right as the last warm color drains from the horizon into deep blue.
funFact: Blue hour gets its color because, at that low sun angle, mostly blue wavelengths of light are left scattering through the atmosphere.

glossary.meaning: The period of twilight just before sunrise or after sunset when indirect sunlight gives the sky a deep blue tone.
The line formed by the highest points along a mountain range or hill chain.

name: Coastal Overlook
description: The sun drops toward the sea through scattered clouds, framed by a forested hillside with the coastline and open water laid out below.
funFact: The gold path stretching across the water toward the sun is called a glitter path — it forms when sunlight reflects off countless small ripples.

glossary.meaning: The shimmering band of reflected light that stretches across water toward the sun, caused by light bouncing off small waves.

name: Waterfront Sunset
description: The sun burns a deep red as it nears the horizon over calm water, silhouetting the structures and treeline along the shore.
funFact: The sun looks red near the horizon because its light has to pass through much more atmosphere at that angle, scattering out the blue wavelengths first.

glossary.meaning: The line where the sky appears to meet the earth or sea, as far as the eye can see.

name: Golden Hills
description: Rolling hills turn deep gold as the low sun rakes sideways across the grass, throwing long shadows down every furrow.
funFact: This raking light is often called the golden hour, and photographers plan entire shoots around the narrow window it lasts.

glossary.meaning: The period shortly after sunrise or before sunset when sunlight is soft, warm, and low in the sky.

name: Waterfall Understory
description: A waterfall cuts through mossy rock in a forest so dense with spray that the air itself seems to glow green.
funFact: The constant mist from waterfalls like this creates its own microclimate, letting moss and ferns grow that couldn't survive anywhere else nearby.

glossary.meaning: A small area with weather conditions noticeably different from the region around it, often caused by local features like water or shade.

name: Open Water Sunset
description: No coastline in sight — just the sun sinking into open water, with waves catching the last color before dark.
funFact: Sunsets over open water often look more vivid than land-based ones, since there's far less dust in the air to dull the color.

glossary.meaning: A stretch of sea or lake far enough from shore that no coastline is visible.
